column1: # topic: Chapter 10: The Opening of America, 1815-1850

column2: A commercial system in which regions sold staple goods to one another for cash and paper money instead of local barter, and manufacturing shifted from master-apprentice workshops to mechanized factories.
The post-War of 1812 economic program that used federal power to foster prosperity in all regions and bind the nation together.

column1: Second Bank of the United States
column2: The nationally chartered bank created to end the financial chaos after the first bank's charter expired.
A mildly protective duty, averaging 20 percent, on imported woolen and cotton cloth, iron, and sugar, meant to shelter American manufacturers.
A duty on imports meant to shelter domestic manufacturers from foreign competition.
Federally supported roads, canals, and bridges meant to bind the nation and move goods.
A machine that let one laborer clean 50 pounds of short-fiber cotton a day instead of 1 pound by hand.
The state-built waterway from Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie that slashed western freight costs and gave New York City dominance in western trade.
Standardized pieces made by machinery so that components could be swapped and goods mass-produced.
An arrangement in which merchants supplied tools and materials to farm families who spun thread or stitched shoe parts at home.
Production in which machinery in one location is tended by unskilled or semiskilled labor, replacing skilled artisan workshops.
The model Massachusetts textile factories that combined paternal supervision with high profits and first employed daughters of New England farm families.
A national organization of craftworkers' unions that blamed monopolies, paper money, machines, and the factory system for degrading labor.
A business form that pools investors' resources and limits individual liability.
State laws that granted a corporate charter automatically to applicants who met minimum qualifications, instead of requiring a special act of the legislature.
The doctrine that Congress may use any appropriate means to carry out a legitimate constitutional end.
The Supreme Court ruling that the Second Bank was constitutional under the "necessary and proper" clause, affirming the doctrine of implied powers.
The Supreme Court ruling that Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce, defined broadly, struck down a New York steamboat monopoly and opened competition.
The Supreme Court ruling that a state land grant is a contract the Constitution forbids states from impairing, even when the grant was obtained by bribery.
The Supreme Court ruling that state charters are contracts, which protected corporations from later state interference.
Farming for cash and credit through regional merchants, with regions specializing in staple crops rather than local self-sufficiency.
Samuel Morse's invention that sent messages instantly over wires and became vital to commerce.
The first major depression in the nation's history, set off when cotton prices and land values collapsed.
